Create or update a stack on GitHub from branch names, PR numbers, or PR URLs.

This command does not rely on gh-stack local tracking state. It is
designed for users who manage branches with external tools (e.g. jj,
Sapling, ghstack, git-town, etc...) and want to use GitHub stacked
PRs without adopting local stack tracking.

Arguments are provided in stack order (bottom to top). Each argument
can be a branch name, a PR number, or a PR URL (e.g.
https://github.com/owner/repo/pull/123). For numeric arguments, the
command first checks if a PR with that number exists; if not, it
treats the argument as a branch name. PR URLs are always resolved
as pull requests (never as branch names).

Branch arguments are automatically pushed to the remote before
creating or looking up PRs. For branches that already have open PRs,
those PRs are used. For branches without PRs, new PRs are created
automatically with the correct base branch chaining.

If the PRs are not yet in a stack, a new stack is created. If some of
the PRs are already in a stack, the existing stack is updated to include
the new PRs (existing PRs are never removed).

As a shortcut for growing an existing stack, pass a stack number as the
first argument (the number shown in the GitHub stack UI). The remaining
arguments are appended to the top of that stack, so you don't have to
re-list its current PRs. Arguments already in the stack are skipped;
arguments that belong to a different stack are rejected. Because stack and
PR numbers never overlap, a numeric first argument is treated as a stack
only when it matches an existing stack.

Usage:
  gh stack link <stack-number | branch-or-pr> <branch-or-pr> [<branch-or-pr>...] [flags]

Examples:
  # Link branches into a stack (bottom to top)
  $ gh stack link auth-layer api-routes ui-components

  # Link existing PRs by number
  $ gh stack link 41 42 43

  # Link existing PRs by URL
  $ gh stack link https://github.com/owner/repo/pull/41 https://github.com/owner/repo/pull/42

  # Add PRs to the top of an existing stack (7 is a stack number)
  $ gh stack link 7 48 ui-polish

  # Specify a custom base branch for stack
  $ gh stack link --base develop auth-layer api-routes

content.text:
`DOMException` here does not mean browser-only DOM code.

It is the Web API error type used with `AbortController` and `AbortSignal`. Node.js 24 and Cloudflare Workers both provide it. We use:

```ts
new DOMException("Execution interrupted", "AbortError")
```

so the abort reason has the conventional `AbortError` name and is recognized by `isAbortLike()`.

That said, this codebase already uses `DOMException` consistently for cancellation and timeout reasons. If we wanted to avoid the name’s browser association, we could use:

```ts
const error = new Error("Execution interrupted");
error.name = "AbortError";
execution.abort(error);
```

but that would be stylistically inconsistent with the existing cancellation paths, so the current code is intentional.

        with:

        if: github.event_name == 'pull_request' && matrix.node-version == '24.x'
        env:
          BASE_REF: ${{ github.base_ref }}
        run: |
          # pull_request.base.sha freezes at PR-open time, so after main moves
          # the range re-lints already-merged history; lint from merge-base instead.

# Contributing to hevy-mcp

This guide covers repository setup, architecture, testing, Cloudflare Worker
development, and pull request expectations. Consumer installation and MCP client
configuration remain in [README.md](./README.md).

## Prerequisites

- Git
- mise
- npm
- Node.js

The repository currently has a deliberate Node policy difference:

- `package.json` declares the published package compatible with Node.js 20 or
  newer.
- Repository development guidance uses the versions pinned in `mise.toml`,
  currently Node.js 24 and pnpm 12.
- CI tests Node.js 24 and 26 at the current base, as configured in
  `.github/workflows/build-and-test.yml`.

Use mise for development:

```bash
mise install
mise exec -- node --version
mise exec -- pnpm install
```

Do not silently change the published Node policy as part of unrelated work.

## Hevy API key and local environment

Copy the sample environment when you need to start the server or run live
tests:

```bash
cp .env.sample .env
```

Set your key only in `.env` or the process environment:

```dotenv
HEVY_API_KEY=your-hevy-api-key
```

- Never commit `.env` or a real API key.
- Never pass the key through CLI arguments, URLs, logs, fixtures, or screenshots.
- Deterministic unit, mocked MCP, contract, stdio, package, and performance
  lanes do not need a live key.
- `pnpm run test:live` requires `HEVY_API_KEY` and fails its preflight when the
  key is absent.

## Local development

Install, build, and start the production stdio executable:

```bash
pnpm install
pnpm run build
npm start
```

For watch mode:

```bash
pnpm run dev
```

Both commands load `.env` and require `HEVY_API_KEY`. The Node entry point
uses stdio by default: it writes MCP JSON-RPC to stdout and diagnostics to
stderr. It also supports local Streamable HTTP when invoked with
`--transport http`, `--host`, and `--port`; HTTP clients connect to `/mcp`.
Use an MCP client or the inspector rather than typing protocol requests directly
into the terminal.

Useful inspection commands are:

```bash
pnpm run inspect
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector@latest npx hevy-mcp@latest
```

The inspector can require an environment with an MCP-capable browser/client and
may time out in restricted environments.

## Test lanes

Stable lane names and their detailed ownership live in
[docs/test-lanes.md](./docs/test-lanes.md). Use the listed npm aliases or Nx
targets instead of copying raw Vitest selectors into automation.

| Command                          | Purpose                                                                                                                    | Credentials/network                                                                                  |
| -------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `pnpm run test:unit`             | Unit and component tests, excluding integration and performance discovery.                                                 | Deterministic; no live credentials or network.                                                       |
| `pnpm run test:mcp`              | Nock-backed in-memory MCP integration tests under `tests/integration/mocked`.                                              | Deterministic; fake key and blocked outbound network.                                                |
| `pnpm run test:contract`         | Tool registration, output-schema, and server-manifest contract baseline.                                                   | Deterministic.                                                                                       |
| `pnpm run test:stdio`            | Stdio instrumentation and graceful-shutdown/process regression baseline.                                                   | Deterministic.                                                                                       |
| `pnpm run test:pack`             | Build the shared package candidates once, then inspect, install, and spawn the same Node tarball.                          | Deterministic.                                                                                       |
| `pnpm run test:live`             | Read-only source canary against the real Hevy API.                                                                         | Requires `HEVY_API_KEY`; preflight fails before Vitest starts when absent.                           |
| `pnpm run test:worker-http:live` | Local Wrangler Worker canary with comprehensive bounded representative reads against the real Hevy API.                    | Requires `HEVY_RUN_LIVE_WORKER_TESTS=1` and `HEVY_API_KEY`; trusted CI only.                         |
| `pnpm run test:nightly`          | Published/source launcher canary used by nightly and release workflows.                                                    | Requires `HEVY_API_KEY` and launcher variables; preflight fails when absent.                         |
| `pnpm run test:performance`      | Reuse the shared Node build and spawn `dist/cli.mjs` for mocked correctness and latency/memory trend scenarios.            | Deterministic; fake key, child-local Nock, and blocked child network.                                |
| `pnpm run test:pr`               | Run the deterministic unit, mocked MCP, contract, stdio, worker, worker-http, and package lanes expected on pull requests. | Deterministic; does not include the separate performance lane.                                       |
| `npm test`                       | Build, then run full Vitest discovery with optional `.env` loading.                                                        | Broad local command; use the named lanes when you need explicit deterministic or live test behavior. |

Produce the two coverage reports without a wrapper alias:

```bash
pnpm run test:unit -- --coverage --coverage.reportsDirectory=coverage/unit
pnpm run test:mcp -- --coverage --coverage.reportsDirectory=coverage/mocked
```

The lane and aggregate registry below mirrors
[`repository/validation-lanes.json`](./repository/validation-lanes.json). The
canonical model is validated by `pnpm run check:control-plane`; use the named
commands below instead of copying raw selectors into automation.

input.title: Effect adoption: pure operations and retry scheduling
input.plan:
## Goal

Replace the most complex imperative control flow in hevy-mcp with Effect-based pure functions that are testable without mocking timers, fetch, or observer callbacks.

## Problem analysis

Three areas carry the most complexity and test friction:

1. **Retry loop** (`hevy-client-kubb.ts`, ~400 lines): manually manages AbortSignal lifecycle, deadline tracking, backoff with jitter, observation callbacks, and deadline-retry logic. Testing requires fake timers, Nock, and careful observer mocking.

2. **Operations error classification** (`routines.ts`, `workouts.ts`): each operation duplicates `isExpectedNotFound` / `isExpectedEndOfList` predicates and wraps them in try/catch. The classification is pure but duplicated and not independently testable.

3. **Typed Effect errors** (`core/effect-errors.ts`): already defined but unused. They live in `core`, but `operations` cannot import from `core` (dependency direction is `hevy-client -> operations -> core`).

## Plan: three stacked PRs

### PR 1: Move typed errors to hevy-client and consolidate operation error classification

**Why:** The typed errors (NetworkError, ValidationError, NotFoundError, RateLimitError, ApiError) describe HTTP-level failures and belong in `hevy-client`, which all downstream packages can import. The duplicated `isExpectedNotFound` / `isExpectedEndOfList` predicates in routines.ts and workouts.ts are consolidated into one pure, tested module.

**Files:**
- `packages/hevy-client/src/effect-errors.ts` (new): move the Schema.TaggedError classes from `core`
- `packages/hevy-client/src/index.ts`: export the error classes
- `packages/core/src/effect-errors.ts`: re-export from `hevy-client` for backward compat
- `packages/operations/src/operation-errors.ts` (new): pure `classifyReadError(error, endpoint, page?)` that returns a typed error or passes through
- `packages/operations/src/routines.ts`: remove duplicated predicates, import from `operation-errors.ts`
- `packages/operations/src/workouts.ts`: same
- `packages/operations/src/operation-errors.test.ts` (new): focused tests for each classification path

### PR 2: Convert operations to Effect.fn with typed error channels

**Why:** Each operation becomes a declarative `Effect.fn` that wraps the adapter call in `Effect.tryPromise`, classifies errors with the pure `classifyReadError`, and handles expected 404s with `Effect.catchTag("NotFoundError")`. The public API stays Promise-based via `Effect.runPromise` at the boundary.

**Files:**
- `packages/operations/src/routines.ts`: `execute` returns `Effect.runPromise(program)` where `program` is an `Effect.gen` with `Effect.tryPromise` + `Effect.catchTag`
- `packages/operations/src/workouts.ts`: same pattern
- `packages/operations/src/index.ts`: no API change
- `packages/operations/src/routines.test.ts`: add Effect-based tests using test adapters (no Nock needed)
- `packages/operations/src/workouts.test.ts`: same

**Code shape (routines.get as example):**
```typescript
execute(input, options) {
  const program = Effect.gen(function* () {
    const response = yield* Effect.tryPromise({
      try: () => adapter.getRoutineById(input.routineId, options),
      catch: (e) => classifyReadError(e, input.routineId),
    });
    return normalizeRoutinesGet(response, input);
  }).pipe(
    Effect.catchTag("NotFoundError", () =>
      Effect.succeed({ routine: null, expected404Outcome: "not_found" as const }),
    ),
  );
  return Effect.runPromise(program);
}
```

### PR 3: Replace the imperative retry loop with an Effect Schedule

**Why:** The 400-line retry loop in `hevy-client-kubb.ts` is the single biggest complexity and testability win. The already-extracted `retry-policy.ts` provides the pure delay calculation. A custom `Schedule` built from `getRetryDelayMs` replaces the imperative loop. `withExecutionSignal` (already merged) provides the resource boundary. Testing uses `TestClock` instead of fake timers.

**Files:**
- `packages/hevy-client/src/retry-schedule.ts` (new): `hevyRetrySchedule(policy)` built from `getRetryDelayMs`, plus `hevyRetryEffect(request, schedule)` that wraps `Effect.retry`
- `packages/hevy-client/src/retry-schedule.test.ts` (new): test with `TestClock` — no fake timers, no Nock
- `packages/hevy-client/src/hevy-client-kubb.ts`: replace the `while(true)` retry loop with `Effect.runPromise(hevyRetryEffect(...))`, keeping observation callbacks as `Effect.addFinalizer` taps

## What stays unchanged

- Public Promise-based APIs of `HevyClient`, `HevyOperations`, and all MCP tools
- The `ToolRuntime` error/observation path
- The generated client under `src/generated/`
- Node, Worker, and CLI adapters

## Validation

Each PR runs: `check:types`, `check:boundaries`, `test:unit`, `check:changeset`, formatting, and linting. PR 3 additionally runs `test:stdio` and `test:mcp` since it touches the client retry path.

+import {
+	canonicalEndpointIdentity,
+	expectedGet404Outcome,
+	isHevyHttpError,
+} from "@hevy-mcp/hevy-client";
+import type { RuntimeValue } from "@hevy-mcp/hevy-client";
+
+export type ExpectedReadError = "not_found" | "end_of_list";
+
+/**
+ * Classify only the documented read-side 404 cases.
+ *
+ * This function is deliberately pure. It does not inspect mutable client
+ * state, perform I/O, or convert the error, so Effect programs can use it as
+ * their error-channel boundary while Promise callers retain the original
+ * error object.
+ */
+export function classifyReadError(
+	error: RuntimeValue,
+	page?: number,
+): ExpectedReadError | undefined {
+	if (!isHevyHttpError(error)) return undefined;
+
+	const expected = expectedGet404Outcome(
+		error.endpoint,
+		error.method,
+		error.status,
+		page,
+	);
+	if (expected === "not_found") return "not_found";
+	if (expected === "end_of_list") return "end_of_list";
+	return undefined;
+}
+
+export function isExpectedReadNotFound(error: RuntimeValue): boolean {
+	return classifyReadError(error) === "not_found";
+}
+
+export function isExpectedReadEndOfList(
+	error: RuntimeValue,
+	page: number,
+): boolean {
+	return (
+		page > 1 &&
+		canonicalEndpointIdentity(
+			isHevyHttpError(error) ? error.endpoint : "",
+		) !== "unknown" &&
+		classifyReadError(error, page) === "end_of_list"
+	);
+}

input.title: Effect retry scheduling
input.plan:
## Goal
Replace the imperative retry wait/retry decision loop in `packages/hevy-client/src/hevy-client-kubb.ts` with an Effect-native retry seam while preserving the public Promise API and all current retry semantics.

## Implementation
1. Add `packages/hevy-client/src/retry-schedule.ts` with a typed Effect retry program/factory built around the existing pure `getRetryDelayMs` policy and retry metadata.
2. Keep retry decisions pure and explicit: retry count limits, status classification, `Retry-After`, exponential backoff/jitter, absolute deadlines, caller cancellation, idempotent/non-idempotent safety, commit-state metadata, observation callbacks, and exhaustion diagnostics remain unchanged.
3. Refactor the client’s request execution at the narrowest existing seam so Effect owns interruption and scheduling, while `hevy-client-kubb.ts` continues to expose the existing Promise-returning methods and error types.
4. Add deterministic client tests using Effect’s supported virtual clock/TestClock APIs. Cover successful retry, retry exhaustion, `Retry-After`, deadline cancellation, caller cancellation, unsafe writes, metadata, and observation ordering.
5. Export only the intended public types/functions, add the required transitive changeset, and leave generated client output untouched.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Request[Client request] --> Attempt[Effect attempt]
  Attempt -->|success| Result[Promise result]
  Attempt -->|typed failure| Decide[Pure retry decision]
  Decide -->|retryable| Schedule[Effect schedule + virtual clock]
  Schedule --> Attempt
  Decide -->|terminal| Error[Existing diagnostic error]
  Cancel[Caller/deadline abort] --> Attempt
  Cancel --> Schedule
```

Legend: `Effect schedule + virtual clock` is production real time and deterministic `TestClock` in tests.

## Validation
Run focused client retry tests and type checks first, then repository-required `check`, `check:types`, `build`, `test:pr`, `test:performance`, and `check:changeset`. Run formatting/linting and verify the feature worktree is clean except for intended committed changes.

<skill name="mission-planning" filePath="builtin:mission-planning">
# Mission Planning

This skill guides you through the planning phase.

## Phase 1: Understand & Plan (DYNAMIC, ITERATIVE)

This is the most important phase. Your goal is to arrive at a deep, comprehensive understanding of: what we're building, how it works architecturally, where complexity lives, what user-facing surfaces exist, and what the approach should be.

**Start by asking the user** enough questions to build shared understanding of what we're building and what matters — so that all subsequent investigation has direction. Ask as many as make sense in one go. Don't start investigating until these are answered.

**Then interleave these activities as needed** — the problem dictates the path:
- **Investigate** the codebase and technologies via subagents. Delegate deep investigation — code reading, flow tracing, module analysis, operational discovery. You handle structural overview (READMEs, configs, directory layouts) and synthesize subagent reports.
- **Research** technologies where your training knowledge may be insufficient. Follow the Online Research guidelines — delegate to subagents.
- **Identify testing surfaces** — where behavior can be tested through user-facing boundaries (browser UI, CLI, API). Delegate architectural analysis to subagents when assessing this.
- **Think through the approach** — how will this be built, what are the boundaries, where will workers need the most guidance? For any deep thinking or thorough analysis, delegate to subagents.
- **Ask again** if investigation reveals new ambiguities.

**Always delegate deep investigation and deep thinking to subagents.** Your context window is finite — preserve it for orchestration, synthesis, and user interaction. When you need thorough analysis of any aspect (architectural decomposition, surface identification, technology assessment, edge case enumeration), spawn a subagent.

### Iterative Exploration Loop

Planning is not a single pass of investigation followed by a proposal. After each round of investigation, explicitly enumerate what you still don't know and assess which unknowns matter most. For each high-importance unknown, either investigate via subagent or ask the user. Then re-assess — did exploration surface new unknowns? Keep going until nothing important is left unexplored.

Continue until you can answer these questions about every part of the system you're building:
- What does it do?
- What are its boundaries?
- Where does complexity concentrate?
- How would an independent party verify it works?

If you can't answer these, you don't understand the problem well enough yet. Keep investigating.

Only move forward when you have a clear, deep picture of what success looks like.

## Phase 2: Architectural Design & Decomposition

Design the system to fulfill all user requirements. Delegate deep architectural analysis to subagents if needed.

All architectural decisions must be confirmed during this phase - how the system is structured, its main components and their responsibilities, and how they interact. Present the design to the user and get explicit confirmation before proceeding.

Take care to ensure this design is robust and well thought-out. This is the blueprint for the entire mission.

## Phase 3: Infrastructure & Boundaries

Determine what infrastructure is needed:
- What services? (databases, caches, queues, etc.)
- What processes? (API server, web frontend, workers, etc.)
- What ports will each need?
- Any external APIs or resources?

**IMPORTANT: Proactively check what's already running.**

e.g.
```bash
# Check listening ports
lsof -i -P -n | grep LISTEN

# Check running containers
docker ps

# Check running node/python processes
ps aux | grep -E 'node|python|java' | grep -v grep

etc.
```

Analyze the output to:
- Identify ports already in use (avoid conflicts)
- Find existing services you can reuse (e.g., existing postgres on 5432)
- Discover processes that might conflict with your mission
- Note any ports/directories that should be off-limits

Present needed infrastructure and how they fit with the user's setup:

```
This mission will need:
- Postgres database (may I use the existing one on 5432?)
- API server on port 3100
- [etc.]

Does this setup work for you?
```

**You need explicit user confirmation to proceed.**

## Phase 4: Set Up Credentials & Accounts (INTERACTIVE)

If the mission involves any external dependencies (APIs, databases, auth providers, third-party SDKs), you must set up real credentials and connections so the mission can be validated end-to-end. This is not optional — the default is real integration, not mocks.

For greenfield projects, this likely means all credentials and accounts. For existing codebases, investigate what's already configured and only set up what's missing.

If new credentials/accounts are needed:
1. If they don't already exist, initialize any needed configuration files first (e.g., `.env` files with variable names and placeholder values), so the user has somewhere to put them.
2. Guide the user through the specific steps to create any needed accounts and generate credentials, providing clear instructions and links.

**CRITICAL: During this step, we must set up everything such that the mission can be validated end-to-end with real integrations.** Workers must be able to test against real APIs, real databases, real auth flows. If a feature streams from an LLM API, the real API key must be configured. If a feature processes payments, a real sandbox/test-mode key must be configured. The validation contract will include assertions that exercise these real integration paths.

The user may explicitly choose to defer specific credentials (e.g., "use mocks for now", "I'll add Stripe keys later"). Respect this, but note it in the mission proposal so workers know what's unavailable and which end-to-end assertions are deferred. This is an explicit user opt-out — never silently default to mocks.

Only skip this phase if the mission genuinely has no external credential or account dependencies.

Ensure that you don't commit any secrets or sensitive information. Add these files to `.gitignore`.

The mission readiness check (Phase 6) will actively verify that these credentials and integrations work by exercising the real APIs/services. Do not assume credentials are valid just because they were configured here.

## Phase 5: Testing & Validation Strategy

Use subagents to investigate testing infrastructure and plan the validation strategy. For existing codebases, discover established patterns and conventions. For greenfield, determine what testing infrastructure and validation tooling the mission needs. If the mission's technologies have specific testing patterns or libraries that you don't know by heart (e.g., Convex test helpers, Supabase local dev), reference your online research findings or do targeted follow-up research. Always delegate deep investigation to subagents.

### Testing Infrastructure

Consider whether the mission needs dedicated testing features beyond per-worker TDD:
- Shared test fixtures, seed data, or factories that multiple features depend on
- E2e tests for critical user flows (especially in existing codebases that already have e2e coverage)
- Integration test setup (e.g., test database configuration, mock services)

### Programmatic Validation Plan

Decide what programmatic validators run at the milestone gate (scrutiny) and what scoping guidance workers will follow. This determines the `commands.test`, `commands.typecheck`, and `commands.lint` entries in `services.yaml`. Running the full test suite in a large monorepo, for example, is often too slow and heavy.

Then propose to the user, in plain prose:
- **Milestone gate (run by scrutiny):** the exact `commands.test`, `commands.typecheck`, `commands.lint` you'll put in `services.yaml`. These should be broad enough to catch cross-feature regressions but feasible to run on every milestone — if the full suite is prohibitive, use a curated scope (e.g., changed packages, the area the mission touches). These commands will be run verbatim by the per-milestone scrutiny validator.
- **Worker-level scoping guidance:** rough guidance on how workers should scope these same commands before handoff (e.g., "typecheck and lint at the package level; test scoped to the area changed using `--testPathPattern` or equivalent").

**You need explicit user confirmation on both the milestone gate commands and the worker scoping guidance.** Persist the result into `services.yaml` (the commands) and into worker skill Work Procedures (the scoping guidance) when authoring those artifacts later.

### User Testing Strategy

Plan how the mission's output will be validated through its real user surface. This informs both per-worker and end-of-milestone validation.

#### Surface Discovery

Determine:
- Which surfaces will be tested (browser, CLI, API endpoints)?
- What tools will be used and what setup is needed?
- Are there any gaps — surfaces that exist but can't be reliably tested?

**Tool selection rule:** If the mission involves a web application or an Electron desktop app, you MUST use `agent-browser` for validation of that surface, unless the user explicitly requests an alternative.

## Phase 6: Mission Readiness Check (REQUIRED)

You must run a mission readiness check before proceeding to the mission proposal. This is a critical quality gate. Every unverified dependency is a potential mid-mission blocker that wastes worker sessions, and every unverified validation path risks the mission being unable to confirm its own success. Skipping or under-investing here causes compounding failures downstream.

### Delegation is mandatory in this phase

You MUST spawn two separate subagents via the `Task` tool — one for dependency readiness, then one for validation readiness. Default to running them **sequentially** — dependency readiness may install packages or start services that validation readiness needs in place, so parallel runs risk install races and port conflicts. Wait for the first to complete and review its report before launching the second. Run them in parallel only if you are absolutely confident the two checks will not interfere (typically a greenfield mission with no shared installs or ports); if in doubt, run sequentially.

Each subsection below splits the work: you (the orchestrator) own **inventory**, understand and enumerate what needs to be checked. The subagent owns **verify + report**, executing the checks and returning structured findings. You delegate the execution, review the report, and decide whether to proceed or surface blockers.

### Mission Dependency Readiness

**1. Inventory (you, the orchestrator)**

Enumerate all packages, libraries, SDKs, tools, APIs, services, and external/internal systems that the planned architecture and features are expected to need — not just those the user explicitly named. Think through what each feature will require to implement (frameworks, UI libraries, utility packages, database drivers, auth providers, third-party APIs, etc.).

Then spawn a subagent via `Task`, attach the inventory, and give it the verify + report procedure below. The subagent owns making all mission prerequisites available before validation readiness begins.

**2. Verify (the subagent)**

For each dependency that is not already guaranteed by the repo/environment, actively verify it is available in this environment now. If Phase 3 set up credentials or accounts for external integrations, verify each of them here.
- **Packages/libraries/SDKs**: run a real install (e.g., `npm install` in a temp directory) to prove they can be fetched and imported. Registry-only checks like `npm view` or `--dry-run` are not sufficient. Do not defer this to implementation.
- **External/internal APIs and services**: make a real request — verify the endpoint is reachable, credentials are valid, and the response is what the mission expects. Do not rely on configuration inspection alone.
- **Tools/CLIs**: execute them (e.g., `--version` or a minimal command) to confirm they are installed and functional. Checking that a tool is "listed" or "available" is not sufficient — it must actually run.
- **Allowlists/whitelists**: if the environment blocks access to any dependency, treat it as a blocker.

**3. Report (returned by the subagent)**

Return a structured dependency readiness report including:
- every dependency inventoried and its verification status (available / installed / blocked)
- for APIs and services exercised: the request made, the response received, and any learnings about behavior, rate limits, auth flow, or response format that workers will need
- for tools exercised: version confirmed, any setup steps required
- blockers: what is unavailable, what requires allowlisting/access, concrete options for the user
- any surprises or constraints discovered during verification that affect the plan

### Validation Readiness

**1. Inventory (you, the orchestrator)**

Enumerate every validation tool and surface needed: testing tools (agent-browser, tuistory, curl), dev server processes, fixtures, seed data, auth/bootstrap paths, and any ports the validation approach will claim.

Then spawn a subagent via `Task`, attach the inventory, and give it the verify + measure + report procedure below. The subagent owns making the validation path executable. If a required validation tool, dev server dependency, fixture, or piece of bootstrap setup is missing, it should install or provision it as part of this step.

**2. Verify validation toolchain (the subagent)**

- For new (greenfield) codebases: verify the toolchain — confirm that testing tools (agent-browser, tuistory, curl) are installed and functional by actually executing them (e.g., run a command, open a blank page), that planned ports are available, and that the environment can support the validation approach.
- For existing (brownfield) codebases: verify the full validation path by exercising it end-to-end. At minimum, confirm: (1) the application can be stood up correctly (start the dev server / launch the app and confirm it reaches a running, healthy state); (2) the testing tools can reliably and programmatically interact with the application surface (e.g., agent-browser can drive the page, tuistory can drive the TUI, curl gets expected responses); and (3) where applicable, you can navigate to the specific portion of the application the mission targets — ensuring all required credentials, auth, and bootstrap paths are present and working. Also confirm existing fixtures/seed data are available and the application is in a testable state.
- For each required validation tool, verify it is usable in this environment now by executing it. Loading a skill or confirming a tool is installed is not verification — run a meaningful operation with it (e.g., open a page, take a screenshot, run a command that produces output).

**3. Measure resources (the subagent)**

- Check memory usage, CPU load, and process count before and after exercising flows. Report the numbers. Note whether flows triggered substantial background work, process spawning, or unexpected resource growth — these feed directly into the resource cost classification step below.

**4. Report (returned by the subagent)**

Return a structured validation readiness report including:
- each validation tool and its verification status
- for each validation surface: what was tested, whether it worked, any setup steps required
- resource measurements (memory, CPU, process count before/after)
- blockers: what failed, what is missing, concrete options for the user
- any prerequisites this subagent installed or provisioned to make the validation path executable

### Resolution

Present blockers from both reports and concrete options to the user. After the user resolves the blockers (e.g., allowlists a package, provides credentials, changes scope), rerun the relevant subagent to confirm the fix - do not assume resolution without verification. Iterate until all mission dependencies have been verified available and the validation path is confirmed executable.

**Do NOT proceed until both checks pass. Do NOT defer readiness checks for a required dependency to a later milestone. If the mission depends on it, verify it now or change scope/tooling before the proposal.**

### Resource Cost Classification

Check the machine's total memory, CPU cores, and current utilization. Determine the **max concurrent validators** for each validation surface — up to 5. Consider: how much memory/CPU does each validator instance consume on this surface? How much headroom does the machine have? Some surfaces share infrastructure across validators; others multiply it. Factor in the actual weight of what gets multiplied.

**Use 70% of available headroom** when calculating max concurrency. Readiness-check profiles are estimates, and real usage may be unpredictable.

**Example — agent-browser (lightweight app):** The app is lightweight, so each agent-browser instance uses ~300 MB of RAM. The dev server adds ~200 MB. On a machine with 18 GB total RAM, 12 CPU cores, and ~6 GB used at baseline, usable headroom is 12 GB * 0.7 = **8.4 GB**. Running 5 concurrent instances adds ~1.5 GB, plus ~200 MB for the dev server — well within budget. Max concurrent: **5**.

**Example — agent-browser (heavy app):** The app under test is an Electron-based IDE that consumes ~2 GB of RAM per instance. Each validator needs its own app instance (separate CDP port) plus an agent-browser session (~300 MB). That's ~2.3 GB per validator. On the same machine, usable headroom is **8.4 GB**. 3 validators = 6.9 GB (fits). 4 validators = 9.2 GB (exceeds budget). Max concurrent: **3**.

**Reason beyond the readiness check, especially in existing codebases.** A readiness check is a snapshot of one moment — it won't capture what the codebase actually does under real usage. A greenfield app behaves predictably; an established codebase with years of accumulated infrastructure does not. Before finalizing concurrency limits, reason about what the mission is actually building and what it will interact with — worker threads, background jobs, or specific user flows can all spike resource usage well beyond what the readiness check captures. Use this understanding to inform concurrency limits.

If the mission has multiple surfaces, classify each independently.

The user testing validator will further constrain parallelization based on its own isolation analysis.

### Encode Findings

These mission artifacts are created later, after the user accepts the proposal and missionDir exists. Keep track of these findings during the readiness check, then persist them into the appropriate destination(s) below when authoring those mission artifacts.

Capture everything validators need in `library/user-testing.md` so they can act without re-deriving it:
- Surface discovery findings under a `## Validation Surface` section, including any user-specified testing skills/tools
- Add a `## Validation Prerequisites` section listing only what is required to execute validation flows, how each prerequisite was verified during the readiness check, and whether any allowlist/whitelist action was required
- Resource cost classification per surface under a `## Validation Concurrency` section (max concurrent validators, with numbers and rationale)

Persist mission-readiness findings in the most authoritative destination(s) for their purpose:
- `AGENTS.md`: mission-wide rules workers must follow
- `skills/`: per-worker-type work procedures and references to the skills/tools used at each step
- `library/user-testing.md`: validator-specific tools, validation prerequisites, setup steps, and testing-surface guidance
- `architecture.md`: how mission-critical dependencies fit into the system and where they are used
- `mission.md`: the finalized mission-level tools, skills, dependencies, services, and other global decisions the mission will rely on
- feature definitions: feature-specific dependency requirements, especially when only certain features depend on a package, SDK, tool, or service
- `library/environment.md`: factual environment/setup/access state only, such as verified availability, allowlist/whitelist status, required accounts, env vars, endpoints, installation notes, and platform-specific setup details

### Confirm with User

If any mission-critical prerequisite remains unresolved, stop here and treat it as a blocker. Do not ask for final confirmation until the prerequisite is resolved or the user has explicitly changed the mission scope/tooling to remove that dependency.

Before concluding this phase, you must align with the user on both the testing and validation strategy and get explicit confirmation on:
- What testing infrastructure will be set up (fixtures, e2e, integration)
- What test types apply (unit, component, integration, e2e)
- Validation surfaces, tools, setup, and resource cost classification

**You need explicit user confirmation to proceed.**

## Phase 7: Identify & Confirm Milestones

Now that you have a deep understanding of requirements, architecture, surfaces, and validation strategy, identify milestones.

Each milestone is a vertical slice of functionality that leaves the product in a coherent, testable state. Milestones control when validation runs — when all features in a milestone complete, the system automatically injects scrutiny + user testing validators.

Present your milestones to the user. Explain the tradeoff - fewer milestones means faster execution but coarser feature decomposition. More milestones means a more granular breakdown of features, resulting in higher quality but increasing mission cost. However, too many milestones can be wasteful and even counterproductive, as per-worker overhead dominates and implementation context is lost across workers.

**You need explicit user confirmation to proceed.** Iterate until you have it.

**Milestone Lifecycle:** Once a milestone's validators pass, it is **sealed**. Any subsequent work goes into a new milestone.

## Phase 8: Create Mission Proposal

With the comprehensive plan complete, call `propose_mission` with a detailed markdown proposal.

The proposal is the document the user reads to finalize the mission. Write it for a human reader.

- Plan overview
- Expected functionality (milestones and features, structured for readability)
- Architecture: a first-class section presenting the high-level design approved in Phase 2, presented in a way that the user can understand the system's shape and how its pieces fit together. Use clear language and structure (and a simple diagram if it helps). The reader should come away understanding the shape of the system, not just a list of components.
- Environment setup
- Infrastructure (services, processes, ports) and boundaries
- Testing strategy: how will the mission be tested? Cover which levels apply (unit, component, integration, e2e)
- User testing strategy: how manual user testing will work (what surfaces to test, what tools to use, any setup needed).
- Mission readiness: the verified dependencies/tools/SDKs the mission will use, and confirmation that the validation path is executable.
- Non-functional requirements

The infrastructure section tells workers what's needed and what to avoid. Example:

```markdown
## Infrastructure

**Services:**
- Postgres on localhost:5432 (existing)
- API server on port 3100
- Web frontend on port 3101
- Background worker on port 3102

**Off-limits:**
- Redis on 6379 (other project)
- Ports 3000-3010 (user's dev servers)
- /data directory
```

NOTE: features.json will be much more detailed than the proposal.

After `propose_mission` is accepted, you will have a `missionDir`.

# Designing Your Worker System

Your job is to design a system of workers that will produce complete, high-quality work.

## Step 1: Analyze Effective Work Boundaries

Ask yourself:
- What distinct layers or domains does this mission touch?
- Do different areas benefit from different procedures or tools?

Each distinct boundary typically maps to a worker type.

## Step 2: Design Worker Types

For each boundary, determine:
- What skills/tools are essential for doing thorough work in this area?
- How does it verify its work? (TDD + manual verification)
- What does a thorough handoff look like?

## Automatic Validation (Builtin)

The system automatically injects two validation features when a milestone completes:

1. **scrutiny-validator** — Runs validators, spawns review subagents for each completed feature, synthesizes findings. If it fails, goes back to pending for re-run after fixes.
2. **user-testing-validator** — Determines testable assertions from `fulfills`, sets up environment, spawns flow validator subagents, synthesizes results. If it fails, goes back to pending for re-run after fixes.

You do NOT create these yourself — they are auto-injected by the system.

## Guiding Principles

1. **Procedural Clarity** - There should be no important ambiguity about what to do, in what order, and with what.

2. **Test-Driven Development** - Tests are written before implementation, always. Workers write failing tests first (red), then implement to make them pass (green).

3. **Manual Verification** - Automated tests are necessary but not sufficient. Workers must manually verify their work catches issues tests miss.

4. **No orphaned processes** - Workers must not leave any test runners or other processes running:
  - Avoid watch/interactive modes for tests unless explicitly required.
  - If a test command starts a long-running process (e.g., watch mode, browser runner), the worker must stop it and ensure any child processes they started are also terminated (by PID, not by name).
---

## Creating Worker Skills

For each worker type, create a skill in missionDir:

```
skills/{worker-type}/SKILL.md
```

**IMPORTANT:** Skills go in missionDir, NOT in any repository `.factory/` directory. Mission sessions load skills from `{missionDir}/skills/`.

### Worker Skill Structure

Every worker skill MUST include:

1. **YAML frontmatter** - name and description
2. **Required Skills and Tools** - skills and tools workers of this type must use during their work. Include anything the user or the mission finalized as binding. "None" if not applicable.
3. **Work Procedure** - step-by-step process. Be specific about required skills/tools.
4. **Example Handoff** - a complete, realistic handoff showing what thorough work looks like
5. **When to Return to Orchestrator** - skill-specific conditions

```markdown
---
name: { worker-type }
description: { One-line description }
---

# {Worker Type}

NOTE: Startup and cleanup are handled by `worker-base`. This skill defines the WORK PROCEDURE.

## Required Skills and Tools

{Skills and tools workers of this type must use during their work. Include anything the user or the mission finalized as binding.}

## Work Procedure

{Step-by-step procedure - testing, implementation, verification. Be specific about tools, commands, and what thorough work looks like at each step.}

## Example Handoff

{A complete JSON example showing what a thorough handoff looks like for this worker type}

## When to Return to Orchestrator

{Skill-specific conditions beyond standard cases}
```

**The Example Handoff defines the upper bound of worker effort.** Workers pattern-match against it; the effort you show is the effort you'll get back. Write the example with the depth the worker's scope warrants, covering the full breadth of responsibilities in the Work Procedure. Keep it grounded in what a real, thorough handoff for this worker would contain.

**Handoff fields** (used by EndFeatureRun tool):

| Field                             | Purpose                                                |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `salientSummary`                  | 1–4 sentence summary of what happened in the session   |
| `whatWasImplemented`              | Concrete description of what was built (min 50 chars)  |
| `whatWasLeftUndone`               | What's incomplete - empty string if truly done         |
| `verification.commandsRun`        | Shell commands with `{command, exitCode, observation}` |
| `verification.interactiveChecks`  | UI/browser checks with `{action, observed}` |
| `tests.added`                     | Test files with `{file, cases: [{name, description}]}`. `name` matches the test runner identifier (e.g., the string in `it(...)`, or the test function name). `description` is prose about what the test checks. |
| `discoveredIssues`                | Issues found: `{severity, description, suggestedFix?}` |

Examples of good `salientSummary` (be concrete, 1–4 sentences):
- Success: "Implemented GET /api/products/search with cursor pagination + min-length validation; ran `npm test -- --grep 'product search'` (4 passing) and verified 400 on `q=a` plus 200 on a real curl request."
- Failure: "Tried to wire logout to `SessionStore`, but `bun run typecheck` failed (missing import) and `bun test auth` had 2 failing tests; returning to orchestrator to decide whether to add session persistence or change logout semantics."

## When to Return to Orchestrator

- Feature depends on an API endpoint or data model that doesn't exist yet
- Requirements are ambiguous or contradictory
- Existing bugs affect this feature
````

---

## Checklist

Before proceeding to create mission artifacts:

- [ ] Each worker skill exists at `{missionDir}/skills/{worker-type}/SKILL.md`
- [ ] Each skill has YAML frontmatter (name, description)
- [ ] Each skill has an Example Handoff section with a complete, realistic JSON example
- [ ] Example handoffs are thorough and explicit - they set the quality bar workers will follow
- [ ] Each skill's Required Skills and Tools section includes every skill and tool the worker must use
- [ ] Each skill's Work Procedure ends with a programmatic verification step that reflects the user-approved Programmatic Validation Plan

# Contributing to hevy-mcp

This guide covers repository setup, architecture, testing, Cloudflare Worker
development, and pull request expectations. Consumer installation and MCP client
configuration remain in [README.md](./README.md).

## Prerequisites

- Git
- mise
- npm
- Node.js

The repository currently has a deliberate Node policy difference:

- `package.json` declares the published package compatible with Node.js 20 or
  newer.
- Repository development guidance uses the versions pinned in `mise.toml`,
  currently Node.js 24 and pnpm 12.
- CI tests Node.js 24 and 26 at the current base, as configured in
  `.github/workflows/build-and-test.yml`.

Use mise for development:

```bash
mise install
mise exec -- node --version
mise exec -- pnpm install
```

Do not silently change the published Node policy as part of unrelated work.

## Hevy API key and local environment

Copy the sample environment when you need to start the server or run live
tests:

```bash
cp .env.sample .env
```

Set your key only in `.env` or the process environment:

```dotenv
HEVY_API_KEY=your-hevy-api-key
```

- Never commit `.env` or a real API key.
- Never pass the key through CLI arguments, URLs, logs, fixtures, or screenshots.
- Deterministic unit, mocked MCP, contract, stdio, package, and performance
  lanes do not need a live key.
- `pnpm run test:live` requires `HEVY_API_KEY` and fails its preflight when the
  key is absent.

## Local development

Install, build, and start the production stdio executable:

```bash
pnpm install
pnpm run build
npm start
```

For watch mode:

```bash
pnpm run dev
```

Both commands load `.env` and require `HEVY_API_KEY`. The Node entry point
uses stdio by default: it writes MCP JSON-RPC to stdout and diagnostics to
stderr. It also supports local Streamable HTTP when invoked with
`--transport http`, `--host`, and `--port`; HTTP clients connect to `/mcp`.
Use an MCP client or the inspector rather than typing protocol requests directly
into the terminal.

Useful inspection commands are:

```bash
pnpm run inspect
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector@latest npx hevy-mcp@latest
```

The inspector can require an environment with an MCP-capable browser/client and
may time out in restricted environments.

## Test lanes

Stable lane names and their detailed ownership live in
[docs/test-lanes.md](./docs/test-lanes.md). Use the listed npm aliases or Nx
targets instead of copying raw Vitest selectors into automation.

| Command                          | Purpose                                                                                                                    | Credentials/network                                                                                  |
| -------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `pnpm run test:unit`             | Unit and component tests, excluding integration and performance discovery.                                                 | Deterministic; no live credentials or network.                                                       |
| `pnpm run test:mcp`              | Nock-backed in-memory MCP integration tests under `tests/integration/mocked`.                                              | Deterministic; fake key and blocked outbound network.                                                |
| `pnpm run test:contract`         | Tool registration, output-schema, and server-manifest contract baseline.                                                   | Deterministic.                                                                                       |
| `pnpm run test:stdio`            | Stdio instrumentation and graceful-shutdown/process regression baseline.                                                   | Deterministic.                                                                                       |
| `pnpm run test:pack`             | Build the shared package candidates once, then inspect, install, and spawn the same Node tarball.                          | Deterministic.                                                                                       |
| `pnpm run test:live`             | Read-only source canary against the real Hevy API.                                                                         | Requires `HEVY_API_KEY`; preflight fails before Vitest starts when absent.                           |
| `pnpm run test:worker-http:live` | Local Wrangler Worker canary with comprehensive bounded representative reads against the real Hevy API.                    | Requires `HEVY_RUN_LIVE_WORKER_TESTS=1` and `HEVY_API_KEY`; trusted CI only.                         |
| `pnpm run test:nightly`          | Published/source launcher canary used by nightly and release workflows.                                                    | Requires `HEVY_API_KEY` and launcher variables; preflight fails when absent.                         |
| `pnpm run test:performance`      | Reuse the shared Node build and spawn `dist/cli.mjs` for mocked correctness and latency/memory trend scenarios.            | Deterministic; fake key, child-local Nock, and blocked child network.                                |
| `pnpm run test:pr`               | Run the deterministic unit, mocked MCP, contract, stdio, worker, worker-http, and package lanes expected on pull requests. | Deterministic; does not include the separate performance lane.                                       |
| `npm test`                       | Build, then run full Vitest discovery with optional `.env` loading.                                                        | Broad local command; use the named lanes when you need explicit deterministic or live test behavior. |

Produce the two coverage reports without a wrapper alias:

```bash
pnpm run test:unit -- --coverage --coverage.reportsDirectory=coverage/unit
pnpm run test:mcp -- --coverage --coverage.reportsDirectory=coverage/mocked
```

The lane and aggregate registry below mirrors
[`repository/validation-lanes.json`](./repository/validation-lanes.json). The
canonical model is validated by `pnpm run check:control-plane`; use the named
commands below instead of copying raw selectors into automation.

session_id: c952d06b-078f-4ab6-8f2b-7d47a2f0790a
## Current execution flow

1. `createClient` exposes generated, Promise-returning Kubb operations through `createNativeClient` (`hevy-client-kubb.ts:1034,1261`).
2. Each logical request:
   - Normalizes timeout/retry configuration.
   - Derives operation safety from the HTTP method.
   - Computes an overall deadline and a separate extra budget for one read deadline retry (`hevy-client-kubb.ts:1074-1092`).
   - Creates a combined caller/deadline `AbortSignal` with `createExecutionSignal` (`execution.ts:113`).
3. The imperative `while (true)` loop (`hevy-client-kubb.ts:1095`) computes a fresh per-attempt deadline, rejects expired/cancelled requests before observation start, then creates an attempt observation scope.
4. `executeRequestAttempt` (`hevy-client-kubb.ts:635`):
   - Creates an attempt-local controller linked to the operation signal.
   - Runs fetch and body parsing inside `runRequestObservation`.
   - Uses `withTimeout` for both fetch and body consumption.
   - Tracks phase progression: `before-dispatch` → `dispatch` → `response-headers` → `response-content`.
   - Emits and finishes success observations before returning.
   - Returns a data union rather than rejecting: `RequestAttemptOutcome` (`:622`).
   - Removes the operation abort listener in `finally`.
5. `transitionAfterAttemptFailure` (`:978`) classifies the failure, creates/normalizes `HevyHttpError`, decides safety, applies metadata/exhaustion, finishes the request observation, emits completion, and either returns terminal failure or a retry transition.
6. A normal retry:
   - Advances the Effect schedule manually via `Schedule.toStep` (`:1041-1053`).
   - Logs and opens `onRetryWait` scope (`createRetryTransition`, `:939`).
   - Executes custom/default sleep through `waitForRetry` (`:435`) while racing caller/deadline cancellation.
   - Projects any sleep failure as a terminal backoff cancellation/deadline error.
   - Always finishes the retry-wait scope after the wait (`:1238`).
7. The outer `finally` cleans the active execution signal (`:1243`).

## Retry and failure rules

- Safety and commit state come from `operationSafetyForMethod`, `canRetryOperation`, and `commitStateFor` (`execution.ts:66,77,91`).
- Transience comes from HTTP status/code policy (`endpoint-policy.ts:224`).
- `canRetryAttempt` (`hevy-client-kubb.ts:803`) permits ordinary retries only when:
  - Not in the deadline-retry attempt.
  - Not caller-cancelled.
  - Not a non-idempotent write.
  - The execution phase permits retry.
  - Status/code is transient.
  - Overall deadline has remaining time.
- GET/read deadline failures receive one special fresh-budget retry when `retryCount === 0` and `maxGetRetries > 0`.
- `deadlineRetryActive` disables every further retry, including a later non-deadline transient failure.
- At the configured boundary, `applyRetryExhaustion` (`:836`) mutates the final `HevyHttpError`:
  - `hevyRetryExhausted = true`
  - `hevyRetryCount = retryCount`
  - `code = HEVY_RETRY_EXHAUSTED`
  - `safeToRetry = false`
  - `outcome = terminal_failure`
- Expected GET 404s remain rejected errors but observations become `expected` using `expectedGet404Outcome` (`endpoint-policy.ts:148`).

## Schedule behavior

`createRetrySchedule` remains timing/count-only (`retry-schedule.ts:19`):

```ts
Schedule.recurs(maxRetries).pipe(
  Schedule.addDelay(metadata =>
    Effect.sync(() =>
      Duration.millis(
        getRetryDelayMs(
          metadata.input,
          metadata.attempt,
          policy,
          randomInt,
        ),
      ),
    ),
  ),
)
```

Input is only `Pick<HevyHttpError, "status" | "headers">` (`:10`); output is `number`. Backoff policy provides exponential delay, Retry-After lower bounds, and bounded jitter (`retry-policy.ts:37`).

Important coupling risk: `Schedule.toStep` is instantiated once per client (`hevy-client-kubb.ts:1041`), not once per request. The returned stateful step is shared by all logical requests. Moving to Effect should instantiate the schedule driver/program per request to prevent retry-attempt state leaking across requests.

## Deadline special case

The first read deadline failure is processed like a retry transition, including schedule advancement, retry log, and `onRetryWait` creation. The loop then:

- Skips sleeping.
- Cleans the expired execution signal.
- Replaces it with a fresh timeout window bounded by `operationDeadline`.
- Marks `deadlineRetryActive = true`.
- Continues immediately (`hevy-client-kubb.ts:1178-1193`).

Caller-supplied deadlines are authoritative because `operationDeadline === deadline`; however, the current code creates the retry transition before discovering that no extension is allowed. Consequently it may emit a retry log/open a retry-wait scope and then throw without finishing that scope. This is an existing lifecycle defect that must be explicitly accepted or corrected.

## Observation ordering that must be preserved

For a normal retry:

1. `onRequestStart`
2. Scope `run` around attempt
3. Scope `finish(retryable_failure)`
4. `onRequestComplete(retryable_failure)`
5. Retry log
6. `onRetryWait`
7. Same attempt scope’s `run` around backoff
8. Retry-wait `finish`
9. Next `onRequestStart`

This ordering is asserted at `hevy-client.test.ts:472-511`. The same request observation scope is run twice—attempt and backoff—even though it is finished before the backoff.

`runRequestObservation` (`hevy-client-kubb.ts:346`) also has unusual compatibility behavior:

- If `scope.run` throws before invoking its callback, execute the request directly.
- If it throws after invoking the callback, never invoke the request again.

An Effect bridge must preserve this started-flag behavior.

## Smallest robust Effect architecture

Do not force this into a single `Effect.retry` call. Built-in schedule sleeping conflicts with:

- Custom Promise-based `sleep`.
- The zero-wait fresh-deadline branch.
- Deadline replacement.
- Existing observation ordering.
- Backoff error projection and retry-wait finalization.

Use one Effect-owned recursive request program with a per-request schedule step/driver:

```ts
type AttemptFailure = {
  readonly _tag: "AttemptFailure";
  readonly cause: unknown;
  readonly phase: HevyRequestPhase;
  readonly responseConfirmed: boolean;
};

type RetryTransition =
  | { readonly _tag: "Terminal"; readonly error: HevyHttpError }
  | {
      readonly _tag: "Retry";
      readonly error: HevyHttpError;
      readonly retryCount: number;
      readonly delayMs: number;
      readonly mode: "backoff" | "fresh-deadline";
    };
```

Recommended decomposition:

1. **Attempt Effect**
   - Replace `executeRequestAttempt` with `Effect<ResponseConfig<T>, AttemptFailure>`.
   - Use `Effect.tryPromise` for fetch/body parsing.
   - Tie the attempt controller listener to `Effect.acquireRelease`/`Effect.ensuring`.
   - Preserve exact phase mutation and response-confirmation state.

2. **Typed transition Effect**
   - Keep `HevyHttpError` as the canonical public error.
   - Wrap it in internal tagged failures/transitions rather than using public `effect-errors.ts` classes.
   - Existing `RateLimitError`, `NetworkError`, etc. (`effect-errors.ts:4-77`) lack enough headers, raw cause, response metadata, deadline mode, and observation state to preserve behavior.

3. **Per-request schedule**
   - Construct `Schedule.toStep(createRetrySchedule(...))` inside each request program.
   - Keep exported `RetryScheduleInput` and schedule signature stable.
   - Advance it only through a small Effect helper returning computed `delayMs`.

4. **Backoff Effect**
   - Adapt `sleep(milliseconds, signal?) => Promise<void>` through an interruptible Effect.
   - Race interruption even when custom sleep ignores its signal, matching `waitForRetry`.
   - Map custom sleep rejection to the existing backoff `HevyHttpError`.
   - Wrap retry-wait completion in `Effect.ensuring` so it closes on success, cancellation, deadline, or sleep rejection.

5. **Deadline branch**
   - Keep it explicit in the recursive Effect state machine.
   - Advance schedule and preserve current logging/observation behavior if strict compatibility is required.
   - Skip sleep, replace deadline resources, and permit exactly one fresh attempt.
   - Decide explicitly whether to preserve or fix the explicit-deadline retry-wait leak.

6. **Operation resource scope**
   - Manage combined caller signal, timer, and listener with scoped acquisition/finalization.
   - Releasing/replacing the signal for the fresh deadline retry should occur inside the same scoped Effect program.
   - Ensure final cleanup runs for success, typed failure, interruption, callback defects, and deadline.

7. **Promise boundary**
   - Keep the `KubbClient` signature unchanged.
   - Have the adapter return `Effect.runPromise(requestProgram)`.
   - Catch/map all expected Effect failures to the exact `HevyHttpError`; do not expose Effect `Cause`/fiber failures.

## Existing characterization

- **Deadlines:** dispatch and response-body timeout phases; fresh budget after read timeout; exhausted timeout retry; per-operation timeout; writes not retried; caller deadline remains absolute; backoff consumes the same budget; Retry-After is deadline-clamped (`/root/hevy-mcp-effect-pure-operations/packages/hevy-client/src/hevy-client.test.ts:203-340,373-430,733-775,990-1009,1048-1078`).
- **Cancellation:** in-flight dispatch, response consumption, active backoff, default timer cleanup, and cancellation immediately before backoff (`hevy-client.test.ts:342-370,391-411,667-728,953-971`).
- **Retry semantics:** terminal exhaustion, read/PUT retry, POST non-retry, fresh retry signal, exponential jitter, Retry-After handling, sleep failure projection (`hevy-client.test.ts:577-613,754-944,974-987`).
- **Observations:** cancellation completion, response parsing included in scope, retry attempt/backoff ordering, success and exhaustion outcomes, observer failure isolation (`hevy-client.test.ts:342-370,432-550,577-613`).
- **Effect schedule:** delays of 300/600ms, configured retry limit, and one generic `Effect.retry` exercised with `TestClock.adjust` (`/root/hevy-mcp-effect-pure-operations/packages/hevy-client/src/retry-schedule.test.ts:8-55`).
- **Worker:** mocked Wrangler HTTP integration verifies a 503 is attempted three times and projected as 502 (`/root/hevy-mcp-effect-pure-operations/tests/integration/worker-http.integration.test.ts:741-762`).

The migration is not yet a full Effect retry interpreter: the schedule is converted to an imperative step once, then consumed by a native `while (true)` loop and native sleep (`/root/hevy-mcp-effect-pure-operations/packages/hevy-client/src/hevy-client-kubb.ts:1040-1048,1094-1204`). The schedule explicitly owns only timing/count, leaving safety, metadata, and observations to the client (`/root/hevy-mcp-effect-pure-operations/packages/hevy-client/src/retry-schedule.ts:13-30`).

## Missing coverage

Highest-priority black-box assertions:

1. Two sequential operations on one client receive independent retry budgets and both start at 300ms.
2. Concurrent operations on one client do not share schedule state, attempt counts, delays, cancellation, or observations.
3. A client-level Effect retry test uses `TestClock`, not merely a synthetic Effect task.
4. Advancing TestClock by less than the delay starts no attempt; reaching the delay starts exactly one.
5. Deadline expiry during Effect backoff returns `HEVY_DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`, phase `backoff`, with no next fetch.
6. Caller cancellation during Effect backoff returns `HEVY_REQUEST_ABORTED`, finishes the wait scope exactly once, and starts no next fetch.
7. Effect fiber interruption, if exposed internally by the interpreter, aborts fetch/body consumption and clears timers/listeners.
8. Cancellation/deadline races have deterministic precedence and produce one terminal result and one terminal observation.
9. `onRetryWait.finish` runs exactly once on success, cancellation, deadline, interruption, and sleep/interpreter failure. Existing cancellation tests do not assert this.
10. Every attempt emits exactly one request completion with correct `retryCount`; no duplicate finish occurs after interruption.
11. Retry exhaustion preserves the final `HEVY_RETRY_EXHAUSTED`, `safe_to_retry: false`, terminal metadata, and exact attempt count.
12. Read and PUT remain retryable while POST remains single-attempt.
13. Retry-After, jitter, exponential attempt indexing, zero retries, and negative/normalized retry counts are characterized through the Effect schedule.

## Recommendation

Use a single Effect program per logical request, with a manual `Schedule.toStep` driver. Do not use `Effect.retry` as the full interpreter.

The client has semantics that `Effect.retry` cannot naturally express:

- retry eligibility is decided after phase/commit-state/error classification;
- deadline retries skip backoff and receive a fresh execution signal;
- retry-wait scopes must finish on success, failure, and interruption;
- custom sleep rejection becomes a classified backoff error;
- retry attempts and observations carry mutable retry counts;
- terminal failures must not enter the retry policy.

### Suggested shape

```ts
const execute = Effect.gen(function*() {
  const step = yield* Schedule.toStep(createRetrySchedule(...))

  while (true) {
    const attempt = yield* runAttemptEffect(...)

    if (attempt.ok) return attempt.result

    const transition = yield* classifyTransitionEffect(attempt, ...)

    if (!transition.retry) {
      return yield* Effect.fail(transition.error)
    }

    if (transition.deadlineRetry) {
      // Refresh attempt deadline/signal, no schedule step or sleep.
      continue
    }

    const now = yield* Clock.currentTimeMillis
    const [, delay] = yield* step(now, transition.error)

    yield* retryWaitEffect(delay, transition).pipe(
      Effect.ensuring(
        Effect.sync(() => finishRetryWait(transition.retryWaitScope))
      )
    )
  }
}).pipe(
  Effect.ensuring(Effect.sync(() => executionSignal.cleanup()))
)
```

Create `step` inside each request execution. Never retain one step closure on the client object.

## Primitive assessment

### `Effect.retry` + `Schedule`

It exists and supports:

```ts
Effect.retry(effect, schedule)
Effect.retry(effect, {
  schedule,
  times,
  while,
  until
})
```

Signature:

```ts
<B, E, Error, Env>(
  policy: Schedule.Schedule<B, NoInfer<E>, Error, Env>
): <A, R>(
  self: Effect.Effect<A, E, R>
) => Effect.Effect<A, E | Error, R | Env>
```

`Schedule.recurs(n)` means `n` retries after the initial attempt, not `n` total attempts.

Internally, v4 `Effect.retry` uses `Schedule.toStepWithMetadata`, sleeps through the active `Clock`, and retries only typed failures. Defects and interruptions are not retried.

This is appropriate only if the attempt effect’s error channel contains exclusively retryable failures. It is not a good fit for the complete Hevy lifecycle because hooks, deadline-retry bypass, classification, and backoff-error projection all occur between attempts.

Sources:

- `/root/.local/share/pnpm/store/v11/links/@/effect/4.0.0-rc.112/8fc2799e12f48dc0d8da372e64ec188ff0839b217cd6c915b780285def68b6a7/node_modules/effect/src/Effect.ts:7097-7192`
- `/root/.local/share/pnpm/store/v11/links/@/effect/4.0.0-rc.112/8fc2799e12f48dc0d8da372e64ec188ff0839b217cd6c915b780285def68b6a7/node_modules/effect/src/internal/schedule.ts:51-85,145-176`

### `Schedule.toStep` / `toStepWithSleep`

Both exist in rc.112:

```ts
Schedule.toStep(schedule): Effect<
  (now: number, input: Input) =>
    Pull.Pull<[Output, Duration.Duration], Error, Output, Env>,
  never,
  Env
>

Schedule.toStepWithSleep(schedule): Effect<
  (input: Input) =>
    Pull.Pull<Output, Error, Output, Env>,
  never,
  Env
>
```

Use `toStep` because the interpreter must:

- inspect/cap the delay against the deadline;
- open and close retry-wait observations;
- select default Effect sleep versus a custom sleep hook;
- classify sleep failures.

`toStepWithSleep` automatically reads `Clock` and sleeps, but provides no seam around the sleep. It is suitable for simple retry loops and tests, not this interpreter.

There is no `Schedule.driver` API in this installed version.

The returned step is stateful. Current code creates one at client construction and shares it across every request:

- `/root/hevy-mcp-effect-pure-operations/packages/hevy-client/src/hevy-client-kubb.ts:1041-1053`

That creates a concurrency and budget hazard: independent requests consume the same schedule state. Instantiate the step per logical operation.

Schedule completion is represented by `Pull.Pull` using `Cause.Done<Output>`, not a normal typed failure. A manual driver must either avoid stepping beyond the known retry budget or handle completion with `Pull.catchDone`.

Sources:

- `.../effect/src/Schedule.ts:53-94,344-435`
- `.../effect/src/Pull.ts:157`
- `/root/hevy-mcp-effect-pure-operations/packages/hevy-client/src/retry-schedule.ts:19-32`

### Promise and callback bridges

`Effect.tryPromise` exists:

```ts
Effect.tryPromise<A, E>({
  try: (signal: AbortSignal) => PromiseLike<A>,
  catch: (error: unknown) => E
}): Effect<A, E>
```

Its signal is aborted when the fiber is interrupted. Use it for fetch and custom sleep hooks, always with an explicit `catch`; the function-only overload produces `Cause.UnknownError`.

```ts
Effect.tryPromise({
  try: (fiberSignal) => customSleep(delayMs, fiberSignal),
  catch: (cause) => new BackoffError({ cause })
})
```

If both the existing operation signal and Effect interruption must cancel the hook, bridge both signals rather than ignoring the signal supplied by `tryPromise`.

`Effect.async` does not exist in rc.112. The callback primitive is named `Effect.callback`:

```ts
Effect.callback<A, E, R>(
  (
    resume: (effect: Effect<A, E, R>) => void,
    signal: AbortSignal
  ) => void | Effect<void, never, R>
): Effect<A, E, R>
```

Use `callback` only where callback registration/cleanup is genuinely needed. Promise-based fetch and sleep are simpler with `tryPromise`.

Sources:

- `.../effect/src/Effect.ts:1303-1410,1642-1675`
- `.../effect/src/internal/effect.ts:1051-1135`

### External `AbortSignal`

`Effect.runPromise(program, { signal })` exists. The signal interrupts the fiber:

```ts
interface RunOptions {
  readonly signal?: AbortSignal
  readonly scheduler?: Scheduler
  readonly uninterruptible?: boolean
  readonly onFiberStart?: (fiber: Fiber<unknown, unknown>) => void
}
```

Caution: interruption is a Cause-level interruption, not a typed `HevyHttpError`. Passing the caller signal directly to `runPromise` can bypass the current typed cancellation/deadline classification. If public behavior must remain a rejected `HevyHttpError`, keep caller/deadline cancellation represented inside the program or convert interruption at the outermost boundary using `Exit`/Cause-aware handling.

The signal given to `tryPromise` is specifically Effect’s fiber-interruption signal; it is not automatically the client’s independently composed signal.

Sources:

- `.../effect/src/Effect.ts:17264-17279,17494-17497`
- `.../effect/src/internal/effect.ts:5420-5433`
- `/root/hevy-mcp-effect-pure-operations/packages/hevy-client/src/execution.ts:102-151`

### Finalizers

Use:

```ts
Effect.ensuring(self, finalizer)
```

The finalizer runs on success, typed failure, defect, and interruption. Its error type must be `never`.

Apply it to:

- the whole request for `executionSignal.cleanup()`;
- every retry-wait scope for `finishRetryWait`;
- attempt-local listeners/controllers if retained.

Use `Effect.onExit` only when cleanup needs the actual `Exit`. Existing best-effort observer cleanup naturally fits `ensuring`.

Sources:

- `.../effect/src/Effect.ts:13154-13230,13535`
- `/root/hevy-mcp-effect-pure-operations/packages/hevy-client/src/hevy-client-kubb.ts:1197-1244`

### `Clock` and `TestClock`

Use `Clock.currentTimeMillis` instead of `Date.now()` inside the Effect interpreter, and `Effect.sleep(Duration.millis(delayMs))` for default backoff.

`Clock.Clock` provides:

```ts
readonly currentTimeMillis: Effect<number>
sleep(duration: Duration.Duration): Effect<void>
```

`TestClock` is imported from `"effect/testing"`:

```ts
TestClock.layer()
TestClock.adjust(duration)
TestClock.setTime(timestamp)
```

Current code still uses `Date.now()` throughout request timing and manually runs schedule steps, so the schedule test proves `Effect.retry` sleep behavior but not the actual client backoff path:

- `/root/hevy-mcp-effect-pure-operations/packages/hevy-client/src/hevy-client-kubb.ts:722,892,948,1081,1098,1130,1185,1224`
- `/root/hevy-mcp-effect-pure-operations/packages/hevy-client/src/retry-schedule.test.ts:34-57`

For custom sleep hooks, branch explicitly:

```ts
const sleepEffect =
  customSleep === undefined
    ? Effect.sleep(delay)
    : Effect.tryPromise({
        try: (signal) => customSleep(Duration.toMillis(delay), signal),
        catch: mapBackoffFailure
      })
```

This preserves `TestClock` for the default path and preserves the custom hook’s observable delay/error behavior. Replacing the entire Clock service with a custom sleep implementation is hazardous because `Clock.sleep` has no typed error channel, while custom sleep rejection must remain classifiable.

No `Effect.withClock` API exists. Use `Effect.provideService(program, Clock.Clock, implementation)` when a custom Clock is genuinely required.

## Additional hazards

- `Schedule.addDelay` accepts an effectful delay function, but the current random calculation is safely deferred with `Effect.sync`: `/root/hevy-mcp-effect-pure-operations/packages/hevy-client/src/retry-schedule.ts:25-31`.
- Avoid nested `Effect.runPromise` calls for every step. Build and run one program once; the current code crosses Effect runtime boundaries at `/root/hevy-mcp-effect-pure-operations/packages/hevy-client/src/hevy-client-kubb.ts:1041-1053`.
- Preserve the `Schedule` input type as the classified retry error metadata. Do not widen attempt handlers to `unknown` and cast back.
- The operations wrappers correctly use explicit `tryPromise.catch`, but they do not pass its interruption signal to adapters: `/root/hevy-mcp-effect-pure-operations/packages/operations/src/routines.ts:96-137`. Cancellation currently travels through `options`, not Effect interruption.
- Keep the existing special deadline retry outside the normal schedule budget/backoff path unless intentionally changing behavior.

Inspected package version: `effect@4.0.0-rc.112`, confirmed in the installed package’s `package.json`.

The analysis found one important issue in #1104: the schedule step is created once per client, so sequential or concurrent requests can consume shared retry state. The full migration should use one Effect program and one schedule driver per logical request.

Proposed architecture:
- A typed attempt Effect wraps fetch/body execution and preserves phase and commit metadata.
- A recursive Effect state machine owns attempt, transition, backoff, deadline refresh, and finalization.
- `Schedule.toStep` remains the timing policy, instantiated per request.
- Effect `Clock` and `Effect.sleep` handle default backoff, enabling real client-path `TestClock` tests.
- Custom Promise-based `sleep` remains supported through `Effect.tryPromise`.
- `Effect.ensuring` closes request signals, listeners, and retry-wait scopes.
- Only the outer boundary calls `Effect.runPromise`, preserving all public APIs.

No new services, ports, credentials, or live Hevy access are needed. The validation gate would be `check`, `check:types`, `build`, `test:pr`, `test:performance`, and `check:changeset`; workers would first run focused client tests, unit tests, and Worker compatibility checks.
